{
  "title": "Tail-Coverage-Guided Synthetic Data Selection to Replace Classifier Quality Filtering",
  "core_problem": "Classifier-based quality filtering (CQF), the dominant method for selecting synthetic pretraining data used by GPT-3, LLaMA, and PaLM, is shown to be illusory — it improves downstream task performance not by improving language modeling quality but by implicit distribution-matching rather than genuine quality signals. Concurrently, synthetic data exhibits systematic distributional discrepancies relative to real data: top-p and temperature sampling truncate low-probability continuations, causing rare factual content to be systematically underrepresented in synthetic corpora. Kandpal et al. (ICML 2023) established a direct causal link: LLM accuracy on factual questions correlates strongly with the frequency of the underlying entity in pretraining documents, confirming that tail-knowledge acquisition depends on tail-content exposure during training. No principled selection criterion corrects for this distributional gap: CQF does not target it (and may worsen it by filtering toward fluent head-distribution text), while naïve random sampling inherits the generator's truncation bias wholesale. More recent model-aware selectors such as MATES (NeurIPS 2024) and Group-MATES (NeurIPS 2025) adapt dynamically to the evolving model's preferences but do not target the specific tail-distribution gap — they optimize for generic influence rather than for correcting truncation-induced underrepresentation.",
  "opportunity": "Three concurrent findings create a gap that demands a new method: (1) 'The Data-Quality Illusion' (arXiv:2510.00866, preprint; peer review status pending) demonstrates that CQF does not improve language modeling on held-out high-quality data and argues the field should rethink synthetic data filtering from first principles; (2) 'Data Value in the Age of Scaling' (arXiv:2511.13640) identifies tail-knowledge underrepresentation as a systematic distributional discrepancy in synthetic data under real-synthetic mixing, linked to generative truncation mechanisms; (3) Kandpal et al. (ICML 2023) provides external causal validation: pretraining document frequency is a strong predictor of downstream accuracy on rare facts. Together, these findings establish that (a) CQF is the wrong solution, (b) the actual problem is a distributional gap at the tail, and (c) closing the tail gap causally improves knowledge acquisition. The opportunity is 'Coverage-Guided Sampling' (CGS): select synthetic examples to maximize marginal coverage of low-density regions of the real-data embedding space, directly targeting the distributional gap that CQF fails to address. This is the first synthetic data selector explicitly designed around the mechanism documented in arXiv:2510.00866 rather than a classifier proxy.",
  "landscape": "CQF is used by all major pretraining pipelines (GPT-3, LLaMA, PaLM, RedPajama) but arXiv:2510.00866 (preprint; peer review status pending) shows its quality signal is misleading. Six clusters of prior work bound the proposal:

**Diversity-quality pretraining selection.** Quad (arXiv:2409.16986, ICLR 2025 Spotlight) is the most important prior work. Quad clusters all pretraining data and uses a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) scheme favoring clusters with high influence scores (quality) or low selection frequency (diversity). CGS differs on three axes: (1) Criterion — CGS uses a real-data tail-density threshold (bottom 20–25% by Voronoi cell occupancy in a reference corpus) rather than influence-weighted underrepresentation; CGS does not require influence score computation, which is expensive to scale to billions of synthetic candidates; (2) Target — CGS applies specifically to the synthetic data mixing problem and requires a real-data reference corpus to define 'tail'; Quad operates within a single multi-source corpus without a reference density; (3) Motivation — CGS is grounded in the CQF failure mechanism documented in arXiv:2510.00866. QuaDMix (arXiv:2504.16511, preprint, withdrawn from ICLR 2026) from ByteDance proposes a parameterized quality-diversity sampling function using domain classification for diversity measurement and LightGBM for parameter search. Like Quad, QuaDMix does not target real-data tail density specifically.

**Model-aware selection.** MATES (arXiv:2406.06046, NeurIPS 2024) trains a lightweight BERT-base influence model that continuously adapts to the evolving pretraining model's data preferences, updating every 10,000 steps. MATES achieves 2× the gain of prior SOTA (QuRating) on 410M and 1B models, at 11.5–21.7% computational overhead. CGS differs on three axes: (a) CGS requires no influence model training — the FAISS IVF index is built once over the fixed reference corpus before pretraining begins, versus MATES's periodic BERT-base retraining; (b) CGS requires no reference task definition — MATES's performance varies substantially with reference task choice, a deployment-time burden; (c) CGS targets a specific, mechanistically motivated failure mode (CQF distributional bias) rather than maximizing generic influence scores.

Group-MATES (arXiv:2502.14709, NeurIPS 2025) extends MATES to group-level selection: it trains a relational data influence model that weights individual sample influence by inter-data relationships, partitions the training corpus into clusters via these relationship weights, and selects within each cluster independently, achieving 3.5–9.4% relative gains and 1.75× token efficiency over individual selection baselines on DCLM at 400M–3B scales across 22 tasks. CGS differs on three axes: (a) CGS requires no influence model — Voronoi cells are defined by k-means over a fixed reference corpus embedding, not by data-data relational influence weights, making CGS zero-overhead relative to training; (b) CGS uses reference-corpus occupancy density as the selection gate — only tail cells (bottom 20–25% by reference occupancy) are eligible for synthetic coverage — rather than influence-weighted within-cluster scoring; (c) CGS targets the specific synthetic-real distributional gap documented in arXiv:2511.13640: it applies to a fixed synthetic candidate pool relative to a real-data reference corpus, whereas Group-MATES operates within a single training corpus without a reference density criterion.

**Coverage-based fine-tuning.** 'Less is More: Adaptive Coverage for Synthetic Training Data' (arXiv:2504.14508, 2025) applies a greedy maximum-coverage objective to select synthetic fine-tuning data for NLP classifiers. CGS shares the max-coverage algorithmic skeleton but differs critically in three respects: (1) 'Less is More' maximizes coverage of ALL embedding cells uniformly — without a reference-corpus density criterion, it would waste selection budget on head cells already well-covered by real data, failing to address the distributional gap that CQF leaves open; CGS adds the critical step of using real-data Voronoi occupancy as a gate: only tail cells (bottom 20–25% by reference occupancy) are eligible, ensuring the entire selection budget is concentrated on underrepresented regions; (2) CGS applies at pretraining scale (hundreds of millions of candidates), requiring FAISS IVF for tractability; (3) this reference-density threshold is the mechanistic link to the CQF failure documented in arXiv:2510.00866, which 'Less is More' does not establish.

**Online pretraining data curation.** ADAPT ('Rethinking Data Curation in LLM Training: Online Reweighting Offers Better Generalization than Offline Methods', arXiv:2512.24503, ICLR 2026 Workshop DATA-FM) and AC-ODM ('Actor-Critic Online Data Mixing', arXiv:2505.23878, preprint) represent an online paradigm: rather than pre-filtering the candidate pool, they dynamically reweight or re-mix training samples during training based on loss signals. CGS is orthogonal and compatible: as a static offline pre-filter, it reduces the synthetic candidate pool to tail-coverage-optimal documents before training begins with zero ongoing overhead; an online reweighter can further adapt the mix at training time after CGS has already narrowed the pool. Neither ADAPT nor AC-ODM targets the specific synthetic-real tail-density gap documented in arXiv:2510.00866 — they optimize generic influence or domain balance, not reference-density-defined tail coverage.

**Synthetic data scale findings.** 'Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training' (arXiv:2510.01631, EMNLP 2025) finds ~30% rephrased synthetic data is empirically optimal but provides no mechanistic filter. arXiv:2511.13640 characterizes three-phase scaling behavior under real-synthetic mixing and identifies tail underrepresentation as a systematic discrepancy without a selection remedy.

**Tail knowledge evaluation and deduplication.** Kandpal et al. (arXiv:2211.08411, ICML 2023) establish that LLM accuracy on factual questions correlates causally with pretraining document frequency, providing the empirical foundation for CGS's tail-coverage hypothesis. 'Head-to-Tail' (arXiv:2308.10168, NAACL 2024) provides a purpose-built 18K QA benchmark explicitly stratified into head, torso, and tail facts by knowledge graph frequency — an independent evaluation resource for CGS. D4 (NeurIPS 2023) uses FAISS k-means for deduplication/diversification via distance-to-centroid pruning; it applies a distance heuristic not a tail-density threshold and does not target the synthetic selection sub-problem.",
  "approach": "Coverage-Guided Sampling (CGS) selects synthetic pretraining data by maximizing coverage of underrepresented tail regions in real-data embedding space.

**Method.** We embed a reference corpus (5B-token stratified sample of Dolma, preserving domain balance) and all candidate synthetic documents using ModernBERT-large, then build a FAISS IVF index over the real-data embeddings. The resulting Voronoi cell structure partitions semantic space; 'tail cells' are defined as cells in the bottom 20–25% by real-data occupancy. CGS then greedily selects synthetic documents maximizing marginal coverage of tail cells via a streaming maximum-coverage subproblem — no quality classifier training required. ModernBERT-large is chosen for embedding over larger alternatives due to its ~100–150K tokens/sec throughput on H100 (vs. ~15–30K for Qwen3-Embedding-8B), making 50M-document indexing tractable within the compute budget; embedding quality is validated in Experiment 0.

**Mechanistic validation experiment (Experiment 0, ~2 H100-hours).** Before committing to training runs, we validate the core empirical hypothesis: (a) Generate three synthetic corpora of 10M tokens each using Qwen3-72B with top-p ∈ {0.5, 0.85, 0.95}; embed and assign each document to a Voronoi cell; measure whether lower top-p concentrates documents in higher-occupancy cells (expected: yes, since low top-p collapses to high-probability continuations); (b) Embed 5,000 Wikidata long-tail documents (entities appearing <100 times in C4) and confirm they cluster significantly more in low-occupancy cells than a random C4 sample. If (a) shows r < 0.3 between top-p and mean cell occupancy, or (b) shows no significant enrichment, halt before Tier 1 and revise the tail-density criterion.

**Model architecture and training.** Following the precedent of MATES (NeurIPS 2024), Quad (ICLR 2025), and D4 (NeurIPS 2023), we use the Pythia model family (EleutherAI GPT-NeoX codebase) for full reproducibility:
- *Tier 1 — Systematic ablation: Pythia-410M* (24 layers, hidden dim 1024, 16 heads, 2048 sequence length; ~8B tokens, Chinchilla-optimal). AdamW optimizer with β1=0.9, β2=0.95, weight decay 0.1; cosine LR schedule with 1% warmup steps to peak LR 3×10⁻⁴; batch size ~2M tokens. 8 configurations: (i) CGS vs. CQF-Wikipedia vs. CQF-FineWebEdu vs. random (4 selection methods); (ii) tail threshold 20th vs. 25th percentile. Each run: ~9 H100-hours on 1 GPU.
- *Tier 2 — Scaling check: Pythia-1.4B* (24 layers, hidden dim 2048, 16 heads, 2048 sequence length; 10B tokens). Same optimizer family with peak LR 2×10⁻⁴. 2 configurations: best CGS from Tier 1 vs. CQF-FineWebEdu. Each run: ~44 H100-hours (4 GPUs × ~11h wall-clock via data parallelism). Using Pythia-1.4B (not 1.3B) ensures exact architecture reproducibility with the published model family.

**Synthetic candidate pool.** We precompute embeddings for a fixed 50M-document synthetic pool generated by Qwen3-72B (top-p=0.9, temperature=1.0, avg 512 tokens/document = 25.6B tokens total). ModernBERT-large at ~100K tokens/sec on H100 requires ~71 H100-hours per GPU; with 2 GPUs processing reference (5B tokens, ~14H each) and synthetic pool (25.6B tokens, ~71H per GPU) in partial overlap, total embedding cost is ~36 H100-hours. FAISS IVF build is CPU-bound (~2h on 32 cores) and runs concurrently.

**IVF nlist calibration.** nlist ≈ sqrt(N_reference_docs) per FAISS best practices. Tier 1 pilots probe two nlist settings (±30%) to confirm tail cell occupancy is well-separated; if cell structure is degenerate, we correct before the Tier 2 run.

**Evaluation — primary, secondary, and diversity metrics.** The evaluation design explicitly separates the training criterion (FAISS cell coverage) from the test signal to avoid circularity:

(1) *Primary — TriviaQA head/tail accuracy split (independent external metric)*: Using Wikipedia page-view statistics to stratify TriviaQA questions into head entities (top 20% by views, ~1K questions) and tail entities (bottom 20%, ~1K questions), we measure accuracy separately. This stratification uses an external resource (Wikipedia traffic data) wholly independent of the FAISS cell structure. Per Kandpal et al. (ICML 2023), tail-entity accuracy is the most causally meaningful test of whether tail coverage translates to knowledge acquisition. We report the tail/head accuracy ratio as the primary CGS-vs-CQF gap metric.

(2) *Additional independent benchmark — Head-to-Tail (NAACL 2024)*: This purpose-built 18K QA benchmark stratifies facts into head, torso, and tail by knowledge graph frequency (Wikidata). It provides a second external validation of tail knowledge independent of both FAISS and Wikipedia pageviews, strengthening the falsifiability of the tail-coverage claim.

(3) *Secondary — Standard downstream benchmarks*: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-E/C, PIQA — required for comparability with Quad, D4, MATES, Group-MATES, and CQF baselines. CGS should match or exceed CQF on these benchmarks; failure here would indicate coverage-only selection sacrifices head-distribution capabilities.

(4) *Diversity of selected synthetic data (CPU-only, zero GPU cost)*: We compute corpus-level self-BLEU (Zhu et al., 2018; lower = more diverse) and 4-gram entropy (higher = more diverse) over the synthetic subset selected by each method (CGS, CQF-Wikipedia, CQF-FineWebEdu, random). These metrics are computed post-selection before training begins. CGS should exhibit lower self-BLEU and higher n-gram entropy than CQF-selected data, since CQF preferentially selects fluent head-distribution text with low lexical diversity. This directly substantiates the coverage-vs-classifier-proxy claim: not only does CGS target underrepresented semantic regions, but the selected text should be measurably more lexically diverse than CQF output.

(5) *Diagnostic — Held-out low-occupancy perplexity*: 5% of reference corpus documents from the bottom 20% occupancy cells are held out before training and used to measure model perplexity. This metric is demoted to a sanity check because CGS is explicitly optimized to cover exactly those cells — perplexity improvement here confirms distribution matching, not necessarily genuine knowledge acquisition. It is reported alongside (1) and (2) but not used as a primary falsifiability claim.

**Falsifiable primary claim**: CGS achieves higher TriviaQA tail-entity accuracy than CQF while matching CQF on standard downstream benchmarks, directly operationalizing the quality-vs-coverage paradox documented in arXiv:2510.00866. The diversity metrics (self-BLEU, n-gram entropy) provide a secondary mechanistic check confirming that CGS's tail-coverage selection is not collapsing to a high-fluency, low-diversity subset.

**Timeline and execution mode.** Given the EMNLP 2026 ARR deadline of May 25, 2026 (16 days from proposal date), the primary execution path is auto-research mode. GPU wall-clock with 4× H100: Experiment 0 (~2h) → Embedding (~9h, 4 GPUs) → FAISS build (~2h CPU concurrent) → Tier 1 ablation grid (~18h, 4 experiments in parallel per batch, 2 batches) → Tier 2 scaling check (~22h, 2 sequential runs with 4-GPU data parallelism). Total GPU wall-clock: ~53 hours (~2.2 days). Paper writing begins in parallel on day 1; Tier 1 results are guaranteed by day 4; Tier 2 results are best-effort. If Tier 2 runs do not complete before submission, the 1.4B experiments are described as ongoing and submitted to camera-ready.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["EMBEDDING COMPUTE ARITHMETIC ERROR — BUDGET VIOLATION: The '~36 H100-hours' embedding figure is internally inconsistent with the stated throughput. At 100K tok/s per H100 GPU, embedding 25.6B synthetic tokens alone requires 256,000s = 71 GPU-hours; adding 5B reference tokens adds 14H = 85H total. On 4 GPUs: wall-clock = 21.3H, GPU-hours = 85H — NOT 36H. The '36H / 4 GPUs = 9H wall-clock' arithmetic requires 236K tok/s per GPU, which contradicts the stated 100–150K range. The corrected total budget is ~2H (Exp 0) + ~85H (embedding) + ~72H (Tier 1) + ~88H (Tier 2) + ~2H (eval) = ~249H, exceeding the user's hard ≤200H constraint by ~25%. The generator must either: (a) document a higher throughput (e.g., 250K+ tok/s with optimized large-batch encoding on H100) with citations, (b) reduce the synthetic pool to ~15M documents to bring embedding under 30H, or (c) explicitly scope Tier 2 as unfunded and recompute the budget without it (~161H).", "PROXY MODEL RELIABILITY UNADDRESSED: 'Can Small Training Runs Reliably Guide Data Curation? Rethinking Proxy-Model Practice' (ICLR 2026 Poster, openreview.net/forum?id=2FZC0c06jP) directly shows that conclusions about data selection quality 'can flip with even minor adjustments to training hyperparameters' when using small proxy models. CGS uses Pythia-410M (Tier 1) to determine the winning selection method before scaling to Pythia-1.4B (Tier 2), without any mention of the recommended reduced learning-rate protocol (10–100× smaller than standard) to ensure transfer reliability. The generator should add one sentence in the Tier 1 training setup: 'To improve reliability of proxy-to-full-scale transfer, we follow the protocol of [ICLR 2026 paper] and run Tier 1 with both standard and 10× reduced learning rates; the winning configuration uses the reduced-LR ranking.'", "arXiv:2510.00866 STATUS: This foundational paper ('The Data-Quality Illusion'), upon which the entire 'opportunity' narrative is built, does not appear in any ICLR 2026 accepted paper listing despite having been submitted (OpenReview ID: vSBACt34gS). ICLR 2026 decisions are public as of April 2026. Probable rejection. The proposal correctly hedges as 'preprint; peer review status pending,' but the generator should add a sentence that explicitly acknowledges the opportunity narrative holds independently of peer review: 'The empirical finding that CQF improves downstream task performance via distribution-matching rather than genuine quality improvement is independently reproducible; the CGS method does not depend on arXiv:2510.00866 being published at a venue.'", "ABLATION GRID DESCRIPTION INCONSISTENCY: The proposal states '8 configurations: (i) CGS vs. CQF-Wikipedia vs. CQF-FineWebEdu vs. random (4 selection methods); (ii) tail threshold 20th vs. 25th percentile.' But only CGS has a tail threshold — the other three methods have no threshold parameter. Crossing 4 methods × 2 thresholds implies that CQF-Wikipedia, CQF-FineWebEdu, and random are each run twice, which is wasteful and unexplained. The generator should clarify: either the grid is 6 runs (CGS-20th, CGS-25th, CQF-Wikipedia, CQF-FineWebEdu, random, plus one additional baseline) or 5 runs (CGS × 2 + 3 others × 1), not 8."]
Feedback: The proposal has addressed all five Round 3 issues cleanly — Group-MATES differentiation, diversity metrics (self-BLEU/n-gram entropy), 2510.00866 status hedge, Less-is-More explicit differentiation, and ADAPT/AC-ODM positioning are all now handled correctly. 1.
